narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 72.8% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is well above the acceptance threshold, your law school application was rejected.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. Your class ranking in the third year of law school was the strongest influence, pushing the prediction strongly toward failure. You placed in the bottom decile (1 out of 10), compared with an average of roughly 5.8 among students who were accepted. This low ranking signaled to the model a high risk that you would struggle on the bar.

Your LSAT score was the second most important factor and also increased the likelihood of failure. At 25.5, it sits well below the 37.2 average of accepted students, indicating weaker preparation in the skills the bar exam tests.

Your undergraduate GPA worked in the opposite direction. At 3.10 it is only slightly below the 3.23 average of accepted applicants, so it modestly pulled the prediction toward passing. However, this positive effect was not large enough to overcome the negative impact of your third-year ranking and LSAT score.

Taken together, these academic signals led the model to conclude that the risk of bar failure was too high for admission. To improve your chances in the future, focus on raising your class ranking through targeted study support and consider retaking the LSAT to demonstrate stronger analytical skills. These steps would directly address the factors that most hurt your current application. (248 words)
